🧠 Smart Filter
Exam-paper / OCR MCQ parser
READY
QUESTION DETECTORS
OPTION DETECTORS
ANSWER / EXPLANATION DETECTORS
Handles wrapped OCR lines, A–D statement blocks, numbered answer choices, “Which of the following…” questions, and an Exp. (1) answer key without mixing the detectors.
Smart Filter reads the plain text you paste in and automatically splits it into questions, options, and answers — even messy text copied from a scanned PDF. Below is every text style it understands, with a sample you can compare your own text against.
15 formats it recognizes, plus your own custom markers
1Starting a new question
Any of these four styles at the start of a line tells Smart Filter "a new question begins here." Pick whichever one matches your source text.
Example 
5. What is the capital of France?
5) What is the capital of France?
[5.] What is the capital of France?
Q5. What is the capital of France?
2Numbered answer choices
If a paper lists its choices with numbers instead of letters, any of these three styles are read as separate options.
Example 
(1) Paris
[2] London
3. Rome
4) Berlin
3Lettered answer choices
The classic A–D style, in any of three punctuation styles. Upper-case and lower-case letters both work, so (a) (b) (c) (d) is read the same way as (A) (B) (C) (D).
Example 
A. Paris
B) London
(C) Rome
(d) Berlin
4Marking the correct answer
Smart Filter looks for a line that names the correct choice, in any of these everyday phrasings.
Example — any one of these 
Exp. (1) Paris has been the capital since 508 AD.
Explanation: [1] Paris has been the capital since 508 AD.
Answer: 1
Correct answer: A
Ans. A
Answer: (a)
5Text that wraps onto extra lines
Long questions or options often break across several lines when copied from a PDF or scan. Smart Filter automatically joins the wrapped lines back into one question or option — it won't mistake a wrapped line for a new question.
Example — reads as one question 
5. Which river flows through both Paris and
Rouen before reaching the sea?
(a) The Seine
(b) The Loire
6"Choose the correct answer" style instructions
Some papers give an instruction line before the choices instead of a plain question. A line like this tells Smart Filter the lettered lines that follow are answer options, not more question text.
Example 
6. Choose the correct answer:
(a) Paris
(b) London
7Two-column answer sheets
Some exam papers print two options per line, side by side, to save space. Smart Filter still reads them in the correct A–D reading order, even though they were printed column-by-column.
Example — printed side by side… 
7. Which of these is NOT a European capital?
(a) Paris        (b) Rome
(c) London       (d) Sydney
…is read back in this order 
(a) Paris  (c) London  (b) Rome  (d) Sydney
8Statements (A)–(D) with numbered answers
Some questions list several lettered statements, then give numbered options that combine those letters — for example "which statements are true." Smart Filter keeps the statements and the numbered combinations separate.
Example 
8. Consider the following statements:
(A) Paris is the capital of France.
(B) Paris is on the river Seine.
(C) Paris is in southern France.
(D) Paris is the largest city in Europe.

(1) (A) and (B) only
(2) (B), (C) and (D)
Exp. (1) Statements A and B are correct.
9Statement / Assertion–Reason questions
A common style in competitive exams: two labelled statements (or an "Assertion" and a "Reason") followed by options that judge whether each one is true. Smart Filter recognizes the labels even when they're written as "Statement I" or spread across a wrapped line, and keeps a reference to a statement inside a normal sentence from being mistaken for a new one.
Example — statements 
9. Statement (A): Paris is the capital of France.
Statement (B): Paris is the smallest city in Europe.
(1) (A) is correct but (B) is wrong.
(2) Both (A) and (B) are correct.
Example — assertion & reason 
10. Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.
Assertion (A): Paris is the capital of France.
Reason (R): Paris is located on the river Seine.
(1) (A) is true but (R) is false.
10Your own custom markers
If your source text uses a format that isn't listed above — a different symbol, prefix, or numbering style — you can type that exact marker into the custom marker fields, and Smart Filter will match it the same way it matches the built-in formats.
Example — a custom marker you define 
Q.5 -> What is the capital of France?
Opt-A: Paris
💡 Good to know: before reading your text, Smart Filter automatically cleans up common scanning/OCR quirks — extra spaces, tabs, curly “smart” quotes, and different dash styles — so slightly messy pasted text still parses correctly.
